claim: Mechanosensitive ion channels convert external mechanical stimuli into electrochemical signals for critical processes including touch sensation, balance, and cardiovascular regulation.
source: Mechanosensitive ion channels convert external mechanical stimuli into electrochemical signals for critical processes including touch sensation, balance, and cardiovascular regulation.
evidence: This is a general statement about mechanosensitive channels supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: MscL opens a wide pore, which accounts for mechanosensitive gating due to in-plane area expansion.
source: The best understood mechanosensitive channel, MscL, opens a wide pore, which accounts for mechanosensitive gating due to in-plane area expansion.
evidence: This statement references established understanding of MscL mechanism, supported by prior research in the field.

claim: Eukaryotic Piezo channels have a narrow pore.
source: Eukaryotic Piezo channels have a narrow pore and therefore must capture mechanical forces to control gating in another way.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented in the manuscript showing pore dimensions and by prior knowledge of Piezo conductance properties.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of mouse Piezo1 was determined in a closed conformation at 3.7Å-resolution.
source: We present a cryo-EM structure of mouse Piezo1 in a closed conformation at 3.7Å-resolution.
evidence: This is directly supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript, including resolution measurements and structural analysis.

claim: The Piezo1 channel is a triskelion with arms consisting of repeated arrays of 4-TM structural units surrounding a pore.
source: The channel is a triskelion with arms consisting of repeated arrays of 4-TM structural units surrounding a pore.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and images presented in the manuscript showing the trimeric architecture.

claim: The shape of Piezo1 deforms the membrane locally into a dome.
source: Its shape deforms the membrane locally into a dome.
evidence: This is supported by both the structural data and the proteoliposome reconstitution experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Membrane tension will alter gating energetics in proportion to the change in projected area under the dome.
source: Quantitatively, membrane tension will alter gating energetics in proportion to the change in projected area under the dome.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on thermodynamic principles and the structural observations, representing a hypothesis.

claim: Piezo1 and Piezo2 are mechanosensitive channels that underlie force-detection in eukaryotic cells.
source: Piezo ion channels, Piezo1 and Piezo2, are mechanosensitive channels (MS channels) that underlie force-detection in eukaryotic cells (Coste et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research establishing the role of Piezo channels.

claim: Piezo channels mediate a large and growing number of cellular processes.
source: The number of cellular processes found mediated by Piezo channels is large and growing at a rapid rate (Eisenhoffer et al., 2012; McHugh et al., 2012; Pathak et al., 2014; Li et al., 2014; Cahalan et al., 2015; Alper, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to research documenting various Piezo-mediated processes.

claim: Piezo channels are responsive in gating to mechanical force.
source: Their essential biophysical characteristics include responsiveness in gating to mechanical force (i.e. mechanosensitivity) and selectivity of the pore for cations (Gnanasambandam et al., 2015; Lewis and Grandl, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior biophysical characterization studies.

claim: Piezo channels are selective for cations.
source: Their essential biophysical characteristics include responsiveness in gating to mechanical force (i.e. mechanosensitivity) and selectivity of the pore for cations (Gnanasambandam et al., 2015; Lewis and Grandl, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior biophysical characterization studies.

claim: Piezo channels transduce mechanical forces into electrical signals in sensory neurons.
source: Together, these characteristics allow Piezo channels to serve their many biological functions, including the transduction of mechanical forces into electrical signals in sensory neurons (Kim et al., 2012; Faucherre et al., 2013; Woo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies demonstrating Piezo function in sensory neurons.

claim: Biophysical studies suggest that Piezo channels sense force directly through the lipid membrane.
source: Biophysical studies suggest that Piezo channels sense force directly through the lipid membrane (Cox et al., 2016; Syeda et al., 2016), although other mechanisms also have been proposed (Lewis and Grandl, 2015; Gottlieb et al., 2012; Peyronnet et al., 2013; Poole et al., 2014; Borbiro et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to biophysical studies, though the statement acknowledges alternative mechanisms have been proposed.

claim: MscL undergoes a large (~20 nm2) in-plane area expansion when it opens.
source: Structural, biophysical and functional analyses show that MscL undergoes a large (~20 nm2) in-plane area expansion when it opens (Perozo et al., 2002; Chang et al., 1998; Sukharev et al., 2001; Corry et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structural and biophysical studies of MscL.

claim: The in-plane area expansion of MscL produces a decrease in the free energy of the membrane-channel system if the membrane is under tension, favoring the open state.
source: This area expansion produces a decrease in the free energy of the membrane-channel system if the membrane is under tension, favoring the open state (Wiggins and Phillips, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to theoretical work on membrane mechanics.

claim: The 20 nm2 physical expansion of MscL determined by structural and biophysical analysis corresponds well to the tension dependence of gating estimated in functional experiments.
source: In MscL the 20 nm2 physical expansion determined by structural and biophysical analysis (Perozo et al., 2002; Sukharev et al., 2001; Corry et al., 2010) corresponds well to the tension dependence of gating estimated in the most carefully executed functional experiments (Chiang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations comparing structural measurements to functional data.

claim: MscL functions as a 'pressure release valve', permitting bacterial survival in the face of osmotic shock.
source: It works well for MscL because that channel functions as a 'pressure release valve', permitting bacterial survival in the face of osmotic shock (Sukharev et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to functional studies of MscL.

claim: MscL has a conductance of approximately 3 nS and complete lack of ion selectivity.
source: The wide pore opening in MscL, associated with a conductance of approximately 3 nS and complete lack of ion selectivity, naturally fits with a large in-plane area expansion and therefore high mechanosensitivity (Sukharev et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to electrophysiological characterization of MscL.

claim: Piezo channels have conductance values around 30 pS.
source: By contrast Piezo channels have conductance values around 30 pS (100 times smaller than MscL) and are cation selective, characteristics that are incompatible with a wide pore (Coste et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to electrophysiological characterization of Piezo channels.

claim: Piezo channels are highly mechanosensitive.
source: Yet Piezo channels are highly mechanosensitive (Lewis and Grandl, 2015; Cox et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to biophysical studies of Piezo mechanosensitivity.

claim: The current structure of mPiezo1 exhibits many differences in molecular detail and global interpretation when compared to an earlier structure.
source: In an attempt to understand how this was accomplished we have determined a structure of the mouse Piezo1 (mPiezo1) channel, which exhibits many differences in its molecular detail and global interpretation when compared to an earlier structure (Ge et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the current structural data to a previously published structure.

claim: The cryo-EM map shows greatest detail near the 3-fold center (local resolution 3.2 Å to 3.6 Å) and less detail near the periphery (local resolution 5 Å to 6 Å).
source: The cryo-EM map shows greatest detail near the 3-fold center (local resolution 3.2 Å to 3.6 Å) and less detail near the periphery (local resolution 5 Å to 6 Å) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is supported by the local resolution analysis shown in the figure and described in the text.

claim: Symmetry expansion with focused refinement improved the map quality, especially at the periphery (local resolution 4 Å to 5 Å).
source: To improve the map quality, symmetry expansion was conducted with focused refinement using a mask covering the central hub and one of the three extended arms. The resulting map showed improvement, especially at the periphery (local resolution 4 Å to 5 Å) (Figure 2f and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the computational analysis and the resulting improved resolution measurements.

claim: A crystal structure (PDB ID: 4RAX) was docked into density corresponding to the C-terminal extracellular domain (CED).
source: A crystal structure (PDB ID: 4RAX) was docked into density corresponding to the C-terminal extracellular domain (CED) and the remaining model (26 TM helices per subunit) was built de novo (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3) (Ge et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the model building procedure using a previously determined crystal structure.

claim: The refined structural model contains 1518 residues (out of 2547), with the N-terminal 576 residues and internal flexible loops missing.
source: The refined structural model contains 1518 residues (out of 2547), with the N-terminal 576 residues and internal flexible loops missing.
evidence: This describes the completeness of the structural model based on the data quality.

claim: The structure's extended arms consist of 24 helices arranged as six repeated 4-TM structural units.
source: The structure's extended arms consist of 24 helices arranged as six repeated 4-TM structural units (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and visualization shown in the figures.

claim: Each 4-TM unit is a left-handed bundle of four helices starting and ending on the intracellular side.
source: Each unit is a left-handed bundle of four helices starting and ending on the intracellular side.
evidence: This describes the structural organization observed in the cryo-EM data.

claim: The six 4-TM repeats assemble with each other as a left-handed helix, causing the extended arms of the triskelion to spiral away from the trimer's center, out of plane with respect to the central pore axis.
source: The six 4-TM repeats assemble with each other also as a left-handed helix, causing the extended arms of the triskelion to spiral away from the trimer's center, out of plane with respect to the central pore axis (Figures 2c,d and 3b).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data showing the three-dimensional arrangement of the repeats.

claim: Adjacent 4-TM repeats are linked by a polypeptide chain that crosses the span of two repeats, owing to their relative orientations.
source: Adjacent 4-TM repeats are linked by a polypeptide chain that crosses the span of two repeats, owing to their relative orientations (Figure 3b).
evidence: This describes the connectivity observed in the structure.

claim: The repetitive pattern of TM helices is well conserved for all six 4-TM units visible in the structure.
source: The repetitive pattern of TM helices is well conserved for all six 4-TM units visible in the structure.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison of the visible 4-TM units.

claim: Sequence analysis suggests that the pattern continues to the N-terminus.
source: Sequence analysis suggests that the pattern continues to the N-terminus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1–3).
evidence: This is based on computational sequence analysis and topology prediction.

claim: A Piezo subunit likely contains nine 4-TM units altogether (the first 3 of which are not visible in the structure) giving a total of 36 TM helices, which form the arms, plus two C-terminal TM helices that meet at the center of the trimer.
source: Therefore, it is likely that a Piezo subunit contains nine 4-TM units altogether (the first 3 of which we do not see) giving a total of 36 TM helices, which form the arms, plus two C-terminal TM helices that meet at the center of the trimer.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed structural pattern and sequence analysis.

claim: The central hub of the trimer is formed by amino acids following TM36.
source: The central hub of the trimer is formed by amino acids following TM36 (Figure 3 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the structural data showing the organization of the central region.

claim: At the center TM37-38 form a 3-fold symmetric channel lined by TM38, capped on the extracellular side by a CED, and extended on the intracellular side by a pore extension (PE) helix.
source: At the center TM37-38 form a 3-fold symmetric channel lined by TM38, capped on the extracellular side by a CED, and extended on the intracellular side by a pore extension (PE) helix (Figure 3a and Figure 6—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: This describes the pore architecture observed in the structure.

claim: TM37-38 are domain-swapped relative to TM1-36.
source: TM37-38 are domain-swapped relative to TM1-36 (Figure 2c).
evidence: This describes the topological arrangement observed in the structure.

claim: The channel is surrounded at the level of the inner membrane leaflet by a layered, helical cuff consisting of 'elbow' helices, a 'base' helix and 'hairpin' helices from all three subunits.
source: The channel is surrounded at the level of the inner membrane leaflet by a layered, helical cuff. The cuff consists of 'elbow' helices (residues 2116 to 2142), a 'base' helix (residues 2149 to 2175) and 'hairpin' helices (residues 2501 to 2534) from all three subunits (Figure 3a and Figure 6—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the cryo-EM map.

claim: The solid cuff attaches the extended arms to the channel.
source: This solid cuff attaches the extended arms to the channel.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural arrangement showing the cuff connecting these regions.

claim: Piezo contains a long intracellular helix of 66 amino acids extending from the trimer center, radially out to TM28.
source: Piezo also contains a long intracellular helix of 66 amino acids extending from the trimer center, radially out to TM28 (Figures 2d and 3).
evidence: This describes a structural feature observed in the cryo-EM map.

claim: The 'beam' feature was observed previously but modeled as two instead of one helix.
source: Referred to as a 'beam', this feature was observed previously (Ge et al., 2015), but modeled as two instead of one helix.
evidence: This compares the current structural interpretation to a previous structure.

claim: Linkers between 4-TM units contain at least one helix that runs perpendicular to the TM helices and to the extended arms.
source: In addition, linkers between 4-TM units contain at least one helix that runs perpendicular to the TM helices and to the extended arms (Figures 2c, 3 and 7b).
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the cryo-EM map.

claim: The 'cross' helices are mostly hydrophobic and located inside of the micelle density, near the intracellular interface.
source: These 'cross' helices are mostly hydrophobic and located inside of the micelle density, near the intracellular interface.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the amino acid composition and location in the structure.

claim: A single subunit of Piezo removed from the trimer can be positioned reasonably well into the plane of a lipid membrane.
source: A single subunit of Piezo removed from the trimer can be positioned reasonably well into the plane of a lipid membrane (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is based on modeling the monomer structure in a planar membrane.

claim: The detergent micelle containing a trimer is curved into a dome shape.
source: However, the detergent micelle containing a trimer is curved into a dome shape (Figures 2b,4b).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cryo-EM data showing the micelle shape.

claim: The diameter of the dome opening is about 18 nm with a depth of about 6 nm.
source: The diameter of the dome opening is about 18 nm with a depth of about 6 nm.
evidence: This is measured from the structural data.

claim: The central cap, formed by the CED, is located mostly inside the dome.
source: The central cap, formed by the CED, is actually located mostly inside the dome.
evidence: This describes the spatial arrangement observed in the structure.

claim: The angle between the central pore axis and the beam in each subunit is about 60° instead of 90°, as would be expected if the trimer were located in a fully flattened membrane.
source: The angle between the central pore axis and the beam in each subunit is about 60° instead of 90°, as we would expect if the trimer were located in a fully flattened membrane (Figures 2d,4b,c).
evidence: This is measured from the structural data and compared to the expected geometry in a planar membrane.

claim: The hydrophobic residues on the TM helices (flanked by charged amino acids) form a clearly curved band on the trimer surface, matching the micelle density.
source: Consequently, the hydrophobic residues on the TM helices (flanked by charged amino acids) form a clearly curved band on the trimer surface, matching the micelle density (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the amino acid distribution and comparison to the micelle density.

claim: The distribution of charged amino acids on the extended arms of Piezo is consistent with the positive inside rule for membrane proteins.
source: The distribution of charged amino acids on the extended arms of Piezo is consistent with the positive inside rule for membrane proteins (von Heijne, 1992).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the charge distribution and comparison to an established principle of membrane protein topology.

claim: The presence of a Piezo channel produces a local dome-shaped deformation of the membrane in small unilamellar vesicles consisting of POPE and POPG.
source: Figure 5a shows a Piezo channel reconstituted into a small unilamellar vesicle consisting of POPE and POPG. The presence of a Piezo channel produces a local dome-shaped deformation of the membrane, with density corresponding to the CED visible inside the dome (the channel is inserted with its extracellular side inside the vesicle).
evidence: This is directly observed in the electron microscopy images of reconstituted vesicles.

claim: The molecular model, without adjustment, conforms to the shape of the locally curved membrane near the Piezo channel in vesicles.
source: The molecular model, without adjustment, conforms to the shape of the locally curved membrane near the Piezo channel (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by overlaying the structural model on the vesicle images.

claim: Vesicles consisting of POPE and POPG tended to be non-spherical even in the absence of Piezo channels, possibly due to the truncated cone and inverted, truncated cone shapes of POPG and POPE lipids, respectively.
source: We observed that vesicles consisting of POPE and POPG tended to be non-spherical even in the absence of Piezo channels, possibly due to the truncated cone and inverted, truncated cone shapes of POPG and POPE lipids, respectively (Israelachvili, 1992).
evidence: This is based on observation of vesicle shapes and knowledge of lipid geometry from the literature.

claim: Vesicles consisting of mixtures of POPC and DOPS, with and without cholesterol, are spherical in shape (circular in projection).
source: Vesicles of these lipid compositions are spherical in shape (circular in projection) (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is directly observed in the electron microscopy images.

claim: In POPC and DOPS vesicles with cholesterol, Piezo channels deform the membrane by producing local membrane curvature.
source: As in POPE and POPG vesicles, Piezo channels deform the membrane by producing local membrane curvature (Figure 5c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the electron microscopy images of reconstituted vesicles.

claim: Piezo channels are almost always inserted with an inside-out orientation in vesicles so that the local curvature (of the dome) matches the global curvature of the vesicle.
source: We note that Piezo channels are almost always inserted with an inside-out orientation in vesicles so that the local curvature (of the dome) matches the global curvature of the vesicle.
evidence: This is based on observation of the orientation of Piezo in the vesicle images.

claim: Piezo deforms lipid bilayers locally into a dome shape.
source: We conclude that Piezo deforms lipid bilayers locally into a dome shape.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the vesicle reconstitution experiments showing membrane curvature.

claim: In cells, the dome will project towards the cytoplasm.
source: In cells, the dome will project towards the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is inferred from the orientation observed in vesicles and the expected membrane topology in cells.

claim: A negatively charged patch of amino acids (E2257, E2258 and D2264) on the CED lies in close contact with a positively charged patch (R1761, R1762 and R1269) located in the extracellular loops of 4-TM units 2 and 3.
source: A negatively charged patch of amino acids (E2257, E2258 and D2264) on the CED lies in close contact with a positively charged patch (R1761, R1762 and R1269) located in the extracellular loops of 4-TM units 2 and 3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the structure showing the spatial proximity and charge distribution.

claim: Hydrogen bonds and salt bridges connect E2257 to R1762 and D2264 to R1761 in a domain-swapped manner.
source: Hydrogen bonds and salt bridges connect E2257 to R1762 and D2264 in R1761 in a domain-swapped manner.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the atomic distances and geometry in the structure.

claim: The electrostatic interactions between the CED and extracellular loops appear to stabilize the trimeric assembly in its curved conformation.
source: These electrostatic interactions appear to stabilize the trimeric assembly in its curved conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of the interactions and their location at the interface.

claim: The transmembrane pore, lined by TM38 and the PE helix, is closed.
source: The transmembrane pore, lined by TM38 and the PE helix, is closed (Figure 6a–c).
evidence: This is based on measurement of the pore radius at the constriction points.

claim: At the level of the membrane inner leaflet, the pore radius at positions E2537, P2536 and M2493 is 0.1 Å, 0.4 Å and 0.3 Å, respectively.
source: At the level of the membrane inner leaflet, the pore radius at positions E2537, P2536 and M2493 is 0.1 Å, 0.4 Å and 0.3 Å, respectively.
evidence: This is measured from the structural data using pore radius calculation.

claim: Estimated from the size of tetraethylammonium (TEA), which is permeable, Piezo should open to a radius of at least 4 Å.
source: Estimated from the size of tetraethylammonium (TEA), which is permeable, Piezo should open to a radius of at least 4 Å (Gnanasambandam et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from functional data on TEA permeability cited from the literature.

claim: Two rings of glutamate residues flanking either side of the narrow region of the pore (E2487 and E2537) likely account for cation selectivity through direct interactions with permeating ions.
source: When it does open, two rings of glutamate residues flanking either side of the narrow region of the pore (E2487 and E2537) likely account for cation selectivity through direct interactions with permeating ions (Figure 6a,c).
evidence: This is inferred from the location of negatively charged residues at the pore constriction and knowledge of ion selectivity mechanisms.

claim: The overall architecture of Piezo's pore shares several similarities with P2X and acid-sensing ion channels (ASIC).
source: The overall architecture of Piezo's pore shares several similarities with P2X (Kawate et al., 2009) and acid-sensing ion channels (ASIC) (Baconguis et al., 2014) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a,b).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison to other channel structures from the literature.

claim: Piezo, P2X, and ASIC are all trimeric.
source: First, all three are trimeric.
evidence: This is based on structural data for all three channels.

claim: The pores of Piezo, P2X, and ASIC contain two TM helices and a large extracellular domain, which enclose a continuous ion-conduction path along the three-fold symmetry axis, including a central vestibule in the extracellular domain.
source: Second, the pores contain two TM helices and a large extracellular domain, which enclose a continuous ion-conduction path along the three-fold symmetry axis, including a central vestibule in the extracellular domain.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison of the three channels.

claim: There are lateral fenestrations located below the extracellular domain and open to the pore in Piezo, P2X, and ASIC, which is the actual ion-conduction path in P2X and ASIC.
source: Third, there are lateral fenestrations located below the extracellular domain and open to the pore, which is the actual ion-conduction path in P2X and ASIC (Kellenberger and Grutter, 2015), and could be the case for Piezo as well.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and citation to literature on P2X and ASIC, with speculation about Piezo.

claim: The two TM helices with an extracellular domain are the core components for a functional and efficient trimeric channel of this type.
source: Given their distinct genetic backgrounds yet similar overall structures, it is reasonable to hypothesize that the two TM helices with an extracellular domain are the core components for a functional and efficient trimeric channel of this type.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural similarities despite different evolutionary origins.

claim: Other components unique to Piezo, including the elbow, base, hairpin, and PE helices, are likely to be directly associated with mechano-transduction.
source: Therefore, other components unique to Piezo, including the elbow, base, hairpin, and PE helices (Figure 3a and Figure 6—figure supplement 1c,d), are likely to be directly associated with mechano-transduction.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural differences between Piezo and the non-mechanosensitive channels P2X and ASIC.

claim: The unique components of Piezo are positioned in a cuff surrounding the narrowest region of the pore and therefore seem well positioned to influence gating.
source: These unique components are positioned in a cuff surrounding the narrowest region of the pore and therefore seem well positioned to influence gating.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural location of these components relative to the pore gate.

claim: Upon mechanical stimulus, major conformational changes are expected in these components in response to movement of the triskelion arms to open the pore.
source: Upon mechanical stimulus, major conformational changes are expected in these components in response to movement of the triskelion arms to open the pore.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the structural arrangement and the proposed mechanism.

claim: Piezo's extended arms project approximately 30° out of the plane defined by the pore, incompatible with a flat membrane.
source: The most strikingly unusual feature of Piezo's structure is that it does not conform to a locally planar membrane. Instead, its extended arms project approximately 30° out of the plane defined by the pore, incompatible with a flat membrane (Figures 2d,4b,c).
evidence: This is measured from the structural data.

claim: The entire structure of Piezo takes the appearance of a 3-sided pyramid – inverted when viewed from outside the cell – that spirals from base to apex to form a semi-sphere-shaped dome (projecting into the cell).
source: The extended arms are also curved so that the entire structure takes the appearance of a 3-sided pyramid – inverted when viewed from outside the cell – that spirals from base to apex to form a semi-sphere-shaped dome (projecting into the cell).
evidence: This describes the overall shape observed in the structural data.

claim: Hydrophobic helices lie perpendicular to the arms like cross bars between the arms, presumably to support the curved membrane as it conforms to Piezo's non-planar shape.
source: Hydrophobic helices lie perpendicular to the arms like cross bars between the arms, presumably to support the curved membrane as it conforms to Piezo's non-planar shape (Figures 2,4,7b).
evidence: This is based on the structural observation and inference about their function.

claim: Twelve N-terminal transmembrane helices are not resolved.
source: Twelve N-terminal transmembrane helices are not resolved.
evidence: This is based on the incompleteness of the structural model.

claim: The N-terminal helices presumably extend the arms even further and appear to coincide with the edge of the dome, far from the center, where the membrane becomes planar again.
source: These presumably extend the arms even further, however, given the curvature of the arms these N-terminal helices appear to coincide with the edge of the dome, far from the center, where the membrane becomes planar again.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed curvature pattern and sequence analysis.

claim: A published low-resolution structure led the authors to conclude that Piezo resides in a locally planar membrane, with extended arms forming extra-membranous, extracellular blades.
source: We note that a published low-resolution structure led the authors to conclude that Piezo resides in a locally planar membrane, with extended arms forming extra-membranous, extracellular blades (Ge et al., 2015).
evidence: This references a different interpretation from a previous structure.

claim: The current structure is fundamentally different from the previous structure in that the arms, composed of transmembrane helices, are inside the membrane and force the membrane to curve.
source: The structure we have described is fundamentally different in that the arms, composed of transmembrane helices, are inside the membrane and force the membrane to curve, as shown in images of Piezo reconstituted into lipid vesicles (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the current structural data and vesicle reconstitution experiments.

claim: If the semi-spherical dome becomes flatter (i.e. more co-planar with the membrane) when Piezo opens, then the channel-membrane system will expand.
source: By appealing to the illustration of mid-plane area expansion in Figure 1, the structure of Piezo offers a plausible explanation for the origin of its tension-gating. If the semi-spherical dome becomes flatter (i.e. more co-planar with the membrane) when Piezo opens, then the channel-membrane system will expand.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural observations and thermodynamic principles.

claim: In MscL, widening of the channel's diameter causes membrane plane expansion.
source: In MscL, widening of the channel's diameter causes membrane plane expansion.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of MscL mechanism.

claim: In the proposed mechanism for Piezo, flattening of the channel and its locally surrounding membrane causes membrane plane expansion by transferring out-of-plane membrane area (the dome) into the membrane plane.
source: In the proposed mechanism for Piezo, flattening of the channel and its locally surrounding membrane causes membrane plane expansion by transferring out-of-plane membrane area (the dome) into the membrane plane.
evidence: This is the proposed hypothesis for Piezo mechanosensitivity.

claim: In both MscL and Piezo, weights are lowered in the 'gravitational analog' (i.e. free energy is reduced).
source: In both cases weights are lowered in the 'gravitational analog' (i.e. free energy is reduced) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is based on thermodynamic principles applied to both mechanisms.

claim: Flattening does not constrain the pore to open wide, so expansion and pore diameter are decoupled such that Piezo can exhibit its small conductance and cation selectivity without compromising the ability to sense lateral membrane tension.
source: Because flattening does not constrain the pore to open wide, expansion and pore diameter are decoupled such that Piezo can exhibit its small conductance and cation selectivity, properties that are essential to its function, without compromising the ability to sense lateral membrane tension.
evidence: This is a key inference from the proposed mechanism explaining how Piezo differs from MscL.

claim: The expanded plane area corresponds quantitatively to the change in area of the dome that is projected onto the membrane plane, ΔAproj, and the resulting energy difference is γ ΔAproj.
source: In this proposed mechanism for Piezo, expansion of the membrane-channel system occurs when a curved, dome-shaped membrane becomes flatter (more planar). The expanded plane area corresponds quantitatively to the change in area of the dome that is projected onto the membrane plane, ΔAproj, and the resulting energy difference is γ ΔAproj (Figure 7c).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on thermodynamic principles.

claim: For the simplified geometry shown in Figure 7 the semi-spherical mid-plane has a total mid-plane surface area of 400 nm2 and a projected area, Aproj, of 280 nm2.
source: For the simplified geometry shown in Figure 7 the semi-spherical mid-plane has a total mid-plane surface area of 400 nm2 and a projected area, Aproj, of 280 nm2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is calculated from the geometric model of the dome.

claim: If Piezo becomes completely co-planar with the membrane when it opens, then ΔAproj associated with opening would be 120 nm2.
source: Therefore, if Piezo becomes completely co-planar with the membrane when it opens (i.e. so that its projected area equals its total area) then ΔAproj associated with opening would be 400 nm2 – 280 nm2 = 120 nm2.
evidence: This is calculated from the geometric model assuming complete flattening.

claim: A membrane under tension γ would favor the open conformation by energy γ ΔAproj, corresponding to 42 kBT stabilization of the open state relative to closed at a membrane tension of only one tenth lytic value (~3.5 kBT/nm2).
source: A membrane under tension γ would thus favor the open conformation by energy γ ΔAproj, corresponding to 42 kBT stabilization of the open state relative to closed at a membrane tension of only one tenth lytic value (~3.5 kBT/nm2), where kB is the Boltzmann constant and T the temperature in degrees Kelvin (Rawicz et al., 2000).
evidence: This is calculated from the projected area change and membrane tension values from the literature.

claim: If Piezo flattens only partially upon opening then ΔAproj will be less than 120 nm2 and the energy difference correspondingly smaller.
source: If Piezo flattens only partially upon opening then ΔAproj will be less than 120 nm2 and the energy difference correspondingly smaller (Figure 7c,d).
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the proposed mechanism.

claim: For MscL, the in-plane area change ΔA is ~20 nm2.
source: Recall that for MscL, the in-plane area change ΔA is ~20 nm2.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of MscL from the literature.

claim: Piezo has the potential for much higher tension sensitivity than MscL.
source: This means Piezo has the potential for much higher tension sensitivity than MscL (equation 2, with ΔA = ΔAproj for Piezo).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the calculated ΔAproj for Piezo to the known ΔA for MscL.

claim: The major origin of tension-dependent gating in Piezo is likely the change in projected area, because it has the potential to be so large.
source: There are other possible origins of tension dependence in Piezo, related to changes in the size, geometry and chemistry of the protein-lipid interface associated with gating (Wiggins and Phillips, 2005; Ursell et al., 2008; Phillips et al., 2012). While these changes are still unknown, we suspect that the major origin of tension-dependent gating is the change in projected area, because it has the potential to be so large.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the magnitude of the calculated projected area change.

claim: There is a separate, intrinsic energy cost to bend a membrane even in the absence of tension.
source: In addition to the tension-dependent energy associated with projected area expansion, there is a separate, intrinsic energy cost to bend a membrane even in the absence of tension (Ursell et al., 2008; Helfrich, 1973; Deserno, 2007; Phillips, 2017).
evidence: This is based on established membrane mechanics theory from the literature.

claim: For the semi-spherical membrane in Figure 7 the magnitude of the bending energy is approximately 150 kBT, even excluding the curvature back into the membrane plane.
source: For the semi-spherical membrane in Figure 7 we calculate the magnitude of this energy to be approximately 150 kBT, even excluding the curvature back into the membrane plane, which will substantially increase the bending energy further (Figure 7—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is calculated using membrane bending theory applied to the geometric model.

claim: The bending energy implies that the Piezo protein must perform work on the membrane to curve it.
source: This bending energy implies that the Piezo protein must perform work on the membrane to curve it.
evidence: This is inferred from the thermodynamic cost of membrane bending.

claim: In the absence of a membrane's tendency toward planarity (i.e. in a detergent micelle) Piezo is very stable in its closed, curved conformation.
source: We propose that in the absence of a membrane's tendency toward planarity (i.e. in a detergent micelle) Piezo is very stable in its closed, curved conformation and we observe physical features – such as surface electrostatic interactions – that support this idea (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the structural observations in detergent.

claim: Inside a membrane Piezo produces similar membrane curvature, but this must occur at the energetic expense of its closed state stability, because some of that energy must go into curving the membrane.
source: Inside a membrane Piezo produces similar membrane curvature, but this must occur at the energetic expense of its closed state stability, because some of that energy must go into curving the membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from thermodynamic considerations of membrane bending.

claim: When tension is applied to the membrane, the additional energy term γ ΔAproj tips the balance, favoring the flatter, open conformation.
source: Then, we propose, when tension is applied to the membrane, the additional energy term γ ΔAproj tips the balance, favoring the flatter, open conformation (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is the core hypothesis of the proposed mechanism.

claim: Lipid membranes of differing stiffness (i.e. different bending moduli) should influence gating through ΔGbend (i.e. stiffer membranes with a more negative ΔGbend should lead to channel opening at smaller values of membrane tension).
source: The equation predicts that lipid membranes of differing stiffness (i.e. different bending moduli) should influence gating through ΔGbend (i.e. stiffer membranes with a more negative ΔGbend should lead to channel opening at smaller values of membrane tension) (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is a testable prediction from the proposed thermodynamic model.

claim: A single subunit is compatible with a planar membrane, whereas the trimer is not.
source: We can only conjecture how changes in Piezo's shape will open the pore. We think it is significant that a single subunit is compatible with a planar membrane, whereas the trimer is not.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis comparing monomer and trimer geometries.

claim: The abrupt angle at which the arms project from the pore implies that forces tending to flatten Piezo will produce the greatest stress at the region of attachment.
source: This is due to the abrupt angle at which the arms project from the pore (Figures 2d,4b,c): this implies that forces tending to flatten Piezo will produce the greatest stress at the region of attachment.
evidence: This is inferred from mechanical considerations of the structural geometry.

claim: The region of attachment coincides with the cuff of helices that surround the pore's narrowest segment, presumably its gate.
source: This region coincides with the cuff of helices that surround the pore's narrowest segment, presumably its gate.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the attachment region and pore location.

claim: A force directed along the triskelion arms toward the center of the trimer, associated with flattening of Piezo's arms, will more likely push the 'swapped' pore-lining helices away from the center and open the pore.
source: At first consideration a force directed along the triskelion arms toward the center of the trimer, associated with flattening of Piezo's arms, might be expected to constrict the pore further. However, given that TM37-38 are domain-swapped relative to TM1-36, such a force will more likely push the 'swapped' pore-lining helices away from the center and open the pore.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the gating mechanism based on the domain-swapped topology.

claim: The membrane dome mechanism does not require the application of a force pressing onto the dome (i.e. a force component normal to the plane of the membrane): lateral membrane tension alone will favor the flatter, opened conformation by a relative energy difference given by γ ΔAproj.
source: In this mechanism a dome of membrane, created by Piezo's shape in its closed conformation, undergoes relative flattening upon channel opening. This mechanism does not require the application of a force pressing onto the dome (i.e. a force component normal to the plane of the membrane): lateral membrane tension alone will favor the flatter, opened conformation by a relative energy difference given by γ ΔAproj.
evidence: This is a key feature of the proposed mechanism distinguishing it from other possible mechanisms.

claim: Whether Piezo interacts directly with cytoskeletal or extracellular matrix proteins to modulate its mechanosensitive gating is unknown.
source: Whether Piezo interacts directly with cytoskeletal or extracellular matrix proteins to modulate its mechanosensitive gating is unknown (Lewis and Grandl, 2015; Gottlieb et al., 2012).
evidence: This acknowledges uncertainty about potential protein-protein interactions, citing relevant literature.

claim: The membrane dome mechanism is a hypothesis inspired by the highly unusual structure of Piezo and its demonstrated ability to curve lipid bilayers into a dome.
source: The membrane dome mechanism presented here is a hypothesis inspired by the highly unusual structure of Piezo and its demonstrated ability to curve lipid bilayers into a dome.
evidence: This explicitly states the speculative nature of the proposed mechanism.

claim: Additional experiments will be needed to test the membrane dome hypothesis.
source: Additional experiments will be needed to test this hypothesis.
evidence: This acknowledges that the hypothesis requires experimental validation.
